common_name: Manhattan II Perennial Ryegrass (Improved Turf-Type Rutgers Lawn Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in early fall or spring; Manhattan II is a Rutgers-derived successor to the original 1960s Manhattan, one of the first turf-type ryegrasses bred for lawns rather than pasture.

directions: Manhattan II refined the original Manhattan perennial ryegrass with a finer leaf blade, denser tillering, and darker green color while keeping the parent cultivar's hallmark trait of germinating and establishing a mowable stand faster than almost any other cool-season turfgrass. It tolerates full sun to light shade and wears well under foot traffic, which has made it a long-standing standard for fall overseeding of dormant bermudagrass athletic fields as well as northern lawns sown alone or blended with bluegrass and fescue. As a bunch-type grass it fills bare patches only by tillering in place rather than spreading, so thin areas need reseeding rather than relying on lateral fill-in. In hot, humid summers it is more prone to gray leaf spot than many newer NTEP-topping ryegrasses, so it performs best kept mowed at a moderate height with good air movement.

common_name: Palmer III Perennial Ryegrass (Third-Generation Fine-Textured Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; Palmer III is the third generation of Pennington's Palmer series, bred for finer texture and improved disease tolerance over the original 1980s Palmer.

directions: Palmer III carries forward the Palmer series' reputation for exceptionally fine leaf texture and rich dark green color while adding improved resistance to brown patch and gray leaf spot compared with the original Palmer released decades earlier. Its rapid germination and seedling vigor make it a favorite for quick fall overseeding of dormant warm-season lawns as well as fast patch repair in cool-season turf, giving usable cover within days of a fall rain or irrigation cycle. It performs best in full sun with regular mowing, forming a dense, wear-tolerant sod that suits both home lawns and moderate-traffic sports turf. Because it is a bunchgrass, thin or damaged areas need overseeding to fill back in rather than relying on rhizome spread.
sources: University of Georgia Extension -- Lawns in Georgia

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; Pennfine was released by Pennsylvania State University in the late 1960s as one of the first ryegrasses bred specifically for fine-bladed lawn turf rather than pasture.

directions: Pennfine is historically significant as one of the earliest turf-type perennial ryegrasses, bred at Penn State to have finer leaves, denser tillering, and better mowing tolerance than the coarse forage-type ryegrasses that had previously been used in lawns out of convenience. Its introduction in the late 1960s helped launch the modern era of turf-type ryegrass breeding that produced later cultivars like Manhattan and Pennfine's own many successors. It germinates and establishes within about a week under favorable conditions, which made it valuable for erosion control and quick cover as well as fall overseeding of dormant bermudagrass. Compared with modern NTEP-topping ryegrasses it shows only moderate resistance to gray leaf spot and red thread, so it is now mainly of historical and breeding-program interest rather than a first choice for new lawns.

common_name: Derby Perennial Ryegrass (Early Turf-Type Fine-Bladed Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; Derby was among the first wave of turf-type perennial ryegrasses released in the late 1970s following Pennfine.

directions: Derby arrived in the late 1970s as part of the second wave of turf-type perennial ryegrasses, offering finer leaf texture, denser tillering, and cleaner mowing quality than the older forage-type ryegrasses it displaced in home lawns. It establishes very quickly from seed, which made it a traditional favorite for fall overseeding of dormant bermudagrass athletic fields and golf course fairways across the transition zone and South. Full sun and regular mowing bring out its best density and color, while heavy shade thins the stand noticeably. As an older-generation cultivar it has only moderate resistance to gray leaf spot and red thread compared with newer NTEP-topping releases, so it has largely been superseded by later ryegrass cultivars for new lawn installations even though it remains a familiar name in turf history.
sources: University of Georgia Extension -- Lawns in Georgia

common_name: Alta Tall Fescue (Original 1940s Oregon Pasture-Type Selection)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or early spring; Alta was one of the two original tall fescue selections released out of Oregon in the 1940s, alongside Kentucky 31.

directions: Alta was one of the first two tall fescue selections brought into cultivation, made from Oregon pasture stands in the 1940s at roughly the same time Kentucky 31 was selected from a Kentucky hillside, and the two founded essentially the entire tall fescue seed industry that followed. It is a coarse-bladed, deeply rooted, drought-tolerant bunchgrass bred and used mainly as pasture and utility turf rather than for fine lawn appearance, and it persists under grazing and low-input mowing far better than most cool-season grasses. Like Kentucky 31 it commonly carries a wild-type fungal endophyte that boosts drought and insect resistance but can be toxic to grazing livestock, so endophyte status matters for pasture use. Modern turf-type tall fescues bred decades later have far finer texture and better mowing quality, but Alta remains historically important as one of the species' two founding selections and is still grown for erosion control, roadside cover, and rough pasture.
sources: Oregon State University -- Tall Fescue (Beaver Turf)
University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension -- Tall Fescue
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Tall Fescue

common_name: Fawn Tall Fescue (Classic 1960s Oregon Pasture and Utility Selection)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or early spring; Fawn was released by Oregon State University in the 1960s as an early alternative to Kentucky 31 for pasture and utility turf.

directions: Fawn was developed at Oregon State University in the 1960s as an earlier-maturing, somewhat finer-bladed alternative to Kentucky 31 for pasture, hay, and utility turf use, and for a time it was among the more widely seeded tall fescues in the Pacific Northwest and similar cool-season regions. It shares tall fescue's deep, drought-resilient root system and tolerance of heat, poor soil, and heavy wear, making it useful for erosion control and low-input cover as well as grazing. Compared with modern turf-type tall fescues bred decades later for lawn appearance, Fawn is coarser in texture and forms a more open, clumpy stand that benefits from regular overseeding to stay dense. It has largely been superseded in home lawns by finer turf-type cultivars but is still referenced in extension variety trials as an older public check cultivar.
sources: Oregon State University -- Tall Fescue (Beaver Turf)
Oregon State University Extension Forage Information System
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Tall Fescue

common_name: Jamestown II Chewings Fescue (Improved Fine-Textured Shade Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall; Jamestown II improves on the original 1970s Jamestown Chewings fescue with denser growth and better disease resistance.

directions: Jamestown II updates the original Jamestown Chewings fescue, one of the first named fine fescue turf cultivars, with tighter tillering, improved density, and stronger resistance to dollar spot and red thread than its 1970s predecessor. As a Chewings fescue it grows in a compact, non-spreading bunch rather than by rhizomes, giving it a fine, upright texture well suited to blending with other fine fescues, ryegrass, or bluegrass in shaded lawn seed mixes. It tolerates dry shade and low-fertility soil markedly better than Kentucky bluegrass or perennial ryegrass, though it thins out under heavy foot traffic since it lacks rhizomes to recover laterally. Sow into a well-drained, lean seedbed in early fall, keep the surface consistently moist through germination, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, which favors disease and reduces the stress tolerance that makes this cultivar useful in the first place.
sources: Oregon State University Extension -- Turfgrass Program

common_name: Reliant IV Hard Fescue (Low-Input NTEP-Tested Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; Reliant IV is the fourth generation of the Reliant hard fescue line bred for low-input turf performance.

directions: Reliant IV continues the Reliant hard fescue line's focus on persistence under minimal mowing, fertilizer, and water, with incremental gains in density, disease resistance, and turf quality over earlier Reliant generations in NTEP low-maintenance trials. It tolerates poor, acidic, or infertile soils and handles dry shade better than Kentucky bluegrass or bermudagrass, making it a common choice for unmowed 'no-mow' meadow plantings as well as traditional low-input lawns. Its fine, wiry leaf texture and slow vertical growth reduce mowing frequency, and it is often blended with other fine fescues for shaded or drought-prone sites. Establish in early fall into a lean, well-drained seedbed, keep the surface moist until germination, and taper irrigation afterward to encourage the deep, tough root system that gives this cultivar its low-input character.
sources: Oregon State University Extension -- Turfgrass Seed Production

common_name: Boreal Creeping Red Fescue (Cold-Hardy Canadian Turf and Reclamation Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or early spring in short-season climates; Boreal is a strongly rhizomatous creeping red fescue bred in Canada for cold hardiness.

directions: Boreal was bred in Canada as a strongly rhizomatous strain of creeping red fescue selected for exceptional winter hardiness, allowing it to persist through the short, cold growing seasons of the northern Prairies and similar climates where many turf species struggle. Its spreading rhizomes let it knit together a self-repairing sod and fill in minor bare or damaged patches, an advantage over the purely bunch-type Chewings and hard fescues. It tolerates dry shade, low fertility, and acidic soil well, and is widely used in low-maintenance lawn mixes, roadside seeding, and reclamation plantings across cold-winter regions. Sow in early fall or, in the shortest-season climates, early spring, keep the seedbed moist through germination, and mow at a moderate to relaxed height since close, frequent mowing reduces its natural density.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada -- Forage and Turfgrass Variety Registration
Oregon State University Extension -- Turfgrass Program
